question: Should you fear death?
summary: Luke 12:4 has Jesus telling his disciples not to fear those who can kill the body, because they have no more power beyond that. John 7:1 then describes Jesus himself avoiding Judea "because the Jews sought to kill him." The teacher who tells his followers not to fear death-threats appears to behave as though he himself takes them seriously enough to avoid the region where the threat is greatest.

reconcile.connective: Commentators explain Jesus's withdrawal from Judea as prudent timing, not fear — distinct from the reckless fear his teaching forbids disciples.

discrepancy.connective: Daniel G. Taylor's BibViz Project (citing EvilBible.com) presses the point: John 7:1 shows Jesus fearing the very death he told disciples not to fear.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing under the heading 'Fear of persecutors — Forbidden / Exemplified' (pp. 277-278), setting Luke 12:4 against John 7:1 verbatim and resolving it: 'Jesus did not shun death, but avoided dying prematurely. When his "hour had come"... he met death with fortitude and composure. To die before the time would have measurably defeated his great purpose.'

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: He had already gone over Galilee four or five times; and he continued there, because he found that the hatred of the Jews was such that they would kill him if they could meet with him in Judea; and his time to suffer was not yet come.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reframes the avoidance of Judea as compliance with a providential timetable ('his time to suffer was not yet come'), not as fear-driven flight, directly answering whether Jesus's own conduct undercuts his teaching.
excerpts.source_note_text:
After these things - St. John passes from the preceding discourse of our Lord, which he delivered a little before the passover, Joh 6:4, to the Feast of Tabernacles, which happened six months after, and thus omits many things mentioned by the other evangelists, which our blessed Lord said and did during that time. He had already gone over Galilee four or five times; and he continued there, because he found that the hatred of the Jews was such that they would kill him if they could meet with him in Judea; and his time to suffer was not yet come.
For he would not walk in Jewry - Instead of this, some MSS., versions, and fathers read, ουγαρ ειχεν εξουσιαν, he had not authority, or liberty to walk, etc. That is, he was no longer tolerated, and could not preach publicly in Judea, but at the risk of his life. He found greater scope for the exercise of his important ministry in Galilee than in Judea, as the chief priests, etc., were continually plotting his death.
